hook.line: Mariana comes in from the street rubbing her hands. Anyone arriving at the café wants you to feel what they just felt.
hook.es: No sabes el frío que hace afuera.
hook.en: You have no idea how cold it is out there.

examples.es: No sabes el frío que hace afuera.
examples.en: You have no idea how cold it is out there.

examples.es: ¡La cara que puso cuando se lo dijiste!
examples.en: The face he pulled when you told him!
The number of people there were!

examples.es: No sabes el hambre que tengo.
examples.en: You have no idea how hungry I am.

examples.es: ¡El ruido que hacían en el hotel anoche!
examples.en: The noise they made at the hotel last night!

examples.es: No sabes el trancón que hay hoy.
examples.en: You have no idea how bad the traffic is today.

rule: To say *how cold* or *how many*, English uses *how* or *what a*. Spanish names the thing first, with its article, then adds *que* and a verb: *el frío que hace*. It works for feelings and amounts too: *el hambre que tengo*, *la cantidad de gente que había*. Open with *No sabes* for a friendly warning, or start straight with the article for an outburst: *¡La cara que puso!* The noun is the star. You already know the adjective version, *lo difícil que es*; this is the noun one.
smallPrint: Teachers call this an exclamative relative clause: an article and a noun, then *que*.

You have no idea how hungry you are.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *el* or *la*: No sabes ___ frío que hace afuera. Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: No sabes el frío que hace afuera.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *la* or *el*: ¡___ cantidad de gente que había! Type the whole sentence.
accept: La cantidad de gente que había

yourTurn.prompt: You have no idea how hungry I am. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: No sabes el hambre que tengo.
yourTurn.why: Name the thing, *el hambre*, then *que* and the verb.

yourTurn.prompt: You have no idea how bad the traffic is today. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: No sabes el trancón que hay hoy.

yourTurn.prompt: The face he pulled when you told him!
yourTurn.answer: ¡La cara que puso cuando se lo dijiste!
accept: La cara que puso cuando se lo dijiste
yourTurn.why: You start with the article and the noun, and the verb comes last.

yourTurn.prompt: Put it in the past: *No sabes el frío que hace afuera.*
yourTurn.answer: No sabes el frío que hacía afuera.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to your friends (you all): *No sabes el hambre que tengo.*
yourTurn.answer: No saben el hambre que tengo.
yourTurn.why: *Saben* is the *ustedes* form; the rest stays.

pitfalls.wrong: No sabes cómo frío hace afuera.
pitfalls.right: No sabes el frío que hace afuera.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English *how cold* does not become *cómo frío*: Spanish names *el frío* and adds *que*.
Don't drop the *que*; it joins the noun to the verb.

pitfalls.wrong: No sabes la hambre que tengo.
pitfalls.right: No sabes el hambre que tengo.
pitfalls.why: *Hambre* is feminine but takes *el* in the singular, like *el agua*.

personal: Imagine coming in from the street. Tell someone what you went through, with *No sabes el...* or *No sabes la... que...*: the cold, the traffic, the hunger.
